title: Vow and Harbor
premise: Xanthe Thornbury has spent twenty years paying down his late father's debts by selling off vineyard parcels one careful acre at a time, keeping only the harbor-facing bakery lease that anchors the town's memory of his family. When Marisol Vega — the woman who wrote him anonymous letters for a decade from prison for a crime she may not have committed — moves into the cottage next door, Xanthe must choose between the loyalty he owes his dead father's version of events and the truth Marisol carries about the fire that ruined them both. As the bakery lease deadline looms and a developer circles, Xanthe uncovers evidence that implicates his own father in the arson, forcing him to forgive himself for twenty years of willful blindness. In the end he testifies to reopen the case, signs the bakery over to a community trust rather than lose it, and chooses Marisol not as penance but as partnership.
about_author: Wendell Hartwell is the pen name of a former small-town newspaper editor who spent fifteen years covering courthouse dockets and county fair pie contests before turning to fiction. He writes romances about people who stay when leaving would be easier, and lives within sight of a working harbor.

chapters.title: The Last Acre
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He signs away another vineyard parcel to cover interest on his father's debts, then walks past the bakery whose lease expires in ninety days. Emotional beat: weary resignation disguised as routine, establishing what 'small safe steps' cost him.

chapters.title: Letters Without a Return Address
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Xanthe's POV: ten years of unsigned letters from prison, each one knowing details of his life no stranger should know. He kept every one. Emotional beat: tenderness tangled with suspicion; the reader learns the letters stopped two years ago without explanation.

chapters.title: The Woman at Number Nine
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She unpacks boxes in the rented cottage beside Xanthe's land, rehearsing and discarding ways to introduce herself. Emotional beat: terror braided with hope; she came back to finish something, not to be forgiven.

chapters.title: Bread and Ashes
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A chance meeting at the bakery ovens turns warm until Marisol says something only the letter-writer could know. Emotional beat: the shock of recognition, and the cowardly lie he tells to escape it.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She recounts, to her probation officer and to us, the night of the winery fire twenty years ago and why she pleaded guilty. Emotional beat: guilt as a load-bearing wall; she protected someone, and it was not herself.

chapters.title: Ninety Days
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The landlord serves notice; a developer named Corliss offers to buy the bakery block and erase Xanthe's debt entirely. Emotional beat: temptation dressed as mercy, and the first flicker of anger that feels like life.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Fence Line
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Xanthe finally confronts Marisol about the letters; she neither denies nor apologizes, asking instead whether he ever wondered who really set the fire. Emotional beat: rupture — he walks away, but for the first time in twenty years he cannot stop thinking.

chapters.title: The Father's Ledger
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Searching his father's study for loan papers, he finds a second ledger with entries dated the week of the fire and a name crossed out: M. V. Emotional beat: vertigo; the ground under his grief begins to shift.

chapters.title: Small Safe Steps
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She works shifts at the diner, avoids Xanthe, and nearly leaves town. A letter arrives — from Xanthis's father, written before his death, unsent. Emotional beat: dread; she realizes the elder Thornbury knew she was innocent and stayed silent.

chapters.title: Two Truths, One Harbor
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Forced together at the town's harvest festival, they trade pieces of the past like contraband. Emotional beat: reluctant intimacy; loyalty to the dead versus loyalty to the living argued openly for the first time.

chapters.title: Corliss Makes His Move
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The developer reveals he knows about Marisol's record and offers to make the problem disappear if Xanthe sells. Emotional beat: cold fury; Xanthe realizes the debt was engineered, and refuses — sealing his own financial ruin.

chapters.title: The Unsent Letter
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She gives Xanthe his father's letter. It confesses the insurance scheme and names an accomplice still in town. Emotional beat: grief curdling into resolve; forgiveness of the dead is harder than forgiveness of the living.

chapters.title: Witness
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He takes the ledger and letter to a retired judge who owes his family nothing and agrees to help reopen the case. Emotional beat: fear of justice outside the law's clock, and the first honest hope.

chapters.title: The Accomplice Next Door
chapters.summary: Dual POV. They identify the accomplice — the beloved town patriarch who now backs Corliss's development. Emotional beat: betrayal on a civic scale; the whole harbor town's memory is built on a lie they helped fund.

chapters.title: Threats in the Vine Rows
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Someone burns a warning in her yard; her parole officer hints her presence is 'complicating things.' Emotional beat: isolation and fear, and Xanthe standing in her doorway refusing to leave.

chapters.title: Lease Day
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The bakery lease expires; instead of signing with Corliss, he transfers the property into a community trust with the judge's help, gutting his own safety net. Emotional beat: liberation through loss; the mirror-forgiveness begins here.

chapters.title: Confession at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Dual POV. On the harbor flats, Xanthe admits he read the trial transcripts years ago, suspected the truth, and chose his father's story because it was easier. Emotional beat: the novel's emotional climax of self-forgiveness; Marisol forgives him not absolution but company.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The reopened-case hearing: testimony, the ledger entered into evidence, the accomplice's lawyer circling. Emotional beat: taut suspense; justice arrives procedural and imperfect, not cinematic.

chapters.title: Exoneration and Its Price
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The conviction is vacated, but the town splits — some apologize, some turn away, and the patriarch's allies retaliate against the trust. Emotional beat: victory that costs; vindication is not the same as belonging.

chapters.title: What We Rebuild
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Together they reopen the bakery under both their names, hiring townsfolk from both sides of the split. Emotional beat: quiet joy; love shown as shared labor rather than declaration.

chapters.title: The First Letter With a Return Address
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Marisol hands him a final letter — signed this time — recounting the decade from her side and asking nothing. He writes back by hand and walks it next door. Emotional beat: tenderness earned; the correspondence becomes conversation.

chapters.title: Vow and Harbor
chapters.summary: Dual POV closing chapter. One year later: the trust holds, the case is closed, and they marry on the bakery steps at dawn with the whole complicated town watching. Emotional beat: resolution — memory honored, truth chosen over loyalty, and a future measured in brave steps together.
